levelDefs.name: Awareness
levelDefs.short: recognises the concept; cannot yet do it.

levelDefs.name: Familiarity
levelDefs.short: can do it from a template, with someone to ask.

levelDefs.name: Proficiency
levelDefs.short: independently delivers usable work on standard pharma problems.

levelDefs.name: Mastery
levelDefs.short: handles non-standard cases; the person others escalate to.

levelDefs.name: Expertise
levelDefs.short: sets the standard; teaches, publishes, or open-sources.

subareas.name: Computational Thinking
subareas.stack: base R, Python stdlib (`itertools`, `functools`, comprehensions), `dplyr` and `purrr` for tidy pipelines; `NumPy`, `SciPy`, `data.table`, and profilers (`profvis`, `microbenchmark`, `timeit`) at higher levels.

examples.text: Cohort matching in a pharmacovigilance database
An ETL pipeline for clinical trial data composed from small pure functions
Real-time pharmacokinetic processing from wearables, profiled and tuned
Approximating drug–target interaction scoring when the exact problem is intractable
A team-adopted internal pattern for reproducible pharma data pipelines

competencies.name: Algorithmic Thinking
descriptions: Recognise loops, conditionals, and recursion in someone else's code and explain in plain language what it does.
Translate a worked algorithm (e.g. sorting adverse events by severity) into Python or R from a tutorial, and predict the result of small changes.
Design and implement an algorithm for a new pharma task (e.g. deduplicating adverse-event reports across sources) without supervision, and document the assumptions.
Notice when the textbook approach won't scale or won't fit messy real data, and choose or adapt a better one (e.g. swap a quadratic match for a hash join when the patient registry grows).
Define the team's algorithmic patterns, contribute to an open-source pharma toolkit, or set the standard others follow.

competencies.name: Functional Thinking
descriptions: Recognise pure functions, immutability, and `map`/`filter`/`reduce` in code; explain why a transformation is "side-effect free".
Use `purrr::map` or Python comprehensions / `functools` to apply a transformation across a list of patient or dosage records, following an example.
Build a functional pipeline end-to-end for a pharma ETL or analysis task (e.g. clinical data harmonisation), composing small pure functions.
Refactor an imperative or fragile pipeline into a robust functional one, parallelise where worthwhile, and explain the trade-offs to the team.
Architect functional patterns that other teams adopt — shared libraries, internal style guide, or open-source contribution.

competencies.name: Complexity Theory
descriptions: Recognise that some pharma problems (cohort matching, dosing optimisation, sequence alignment) get expensive fast, and tell "feasible" from "intractable" at a high level.
Use `timeit` or `microbenchmark` to measure runtime on a small dataset and notice when growth looks non-linear.
Compare candidate algorithms on big-O grounds and pick the right one for the data size at hand (when to index, when to stream, when a join is the wrong shape).
Recognise NP-hard structure in a real pharma problem (drug–target scoring, scheduling, study design) and choose an approximation, heuristic, or sampling strategy with a defensible guarantee.
Advance the practice — publish, contribute novel heuristics, or set up a standard approach for hard problems that the wider org adopts.

subareas.name: Computing & Computing Systems
subareas.stack: local Linux/macOS shell, Python and R runtimes; AWS / GCP / Azure managed services (S3/BigQuery/EFS), containers (Docker), batch and Spark-style frameworks (`pyspark`, `arrow`, `duckdb`, `data.table`) for large data.

examples.text: Running a clinical-trial analysis from a local laptop without breaking reproducibility
Lifting an analysis pipeline into a managed cloud workspace with controlled patient-data access
Recognising when a pharmacovigilance dataset has outgrown the laptop and a big-data system is needed
Running a multi-million-row genomics or claims analysis on Spark / DuckDB / Arrow with sensible partitioning

competencies.name: Computing & Computer Fundamentals
descriptions: Explain what files, processes, memory, and an operating system are, and where electronic health records live in that picture.
Use the shell to navigate, copy, and run scripts; explain the difference between local and shared storage for patient data.
Set up a working pharma analysis environment (Python or R, virtualenv/renv, dependencies) and run analyses reproducibly on a laptop.
Diagnose performance, memory, and permission issues that block a pharma pipeline; choose appropriate hardware and storage for the workload.
Set engineering standards for the team's compute environments and tooling.

competencies.name: Cloud Computing
descriptions: Explain what a cloud provider offers (compute, storage, identity) and why pharma workloads often run there under access controls.
Spin up a managed notebook or VM in a sandbox tenant and run a small analysis, following an internal guide.
Run a real pharma analysis end-to-end in a controlled cloud workspace, including managed storage and access policies.
Design a cost- and access-aware cloud setup for a pharma project: storage tiers, IAM, regions for residency, audit trails.
Define the team's reference cloud architecture for regulated pharma data, or contribute to organisation-level patterns.

competencies.name: Big Data Systems (Concept Introduction)
descriptions: Recognise terms (Spark, Hadoop, MPP, columnar storage, partitioning) and explain at a high level when "big" matters in pharma.
Read an existing big-data pipeline diagram or notebook and explain its main steps.
Decide, given a pharma dataset, whether a single-machine tool (`data.table`, `duckdb`, `arrow`) suffices or a distributed system is warranted.
— *(merges with Big Data Systems (Application) at this level)*
— *(merges with Big Data Systems (Application) at this level)*

competencies.name: Big Data Systems (Application)
descriptions: — *(introduced via the Concept Introduction competency)*
Run a small Spark, BigQuery, or DuckDB job on a sample dataset following an example.
Implement a pharma analysis on a large dataset (claims, registries, omics) using a distributed engine, with sensible partitioning and joins.
Tune real workloads — diagnose skew, broadcast joins, push-down predicates, choose file formats — for cost and latency on realistic pharma data.
Architect the team's big-data patterns and platform choices for pharma scale.

subareas.name: Programming
subareas.stack: Python (with `numpy`, `pandas`, `pytest`), R (`tidyverse`, `data.table`, `testthat`); Quarto / R Markdown / Jupyter for literate analysis; LLM coding assistants (Copilot, Claude, Cursor) at L2+; profilers and benchmarks (`profvis`, `microbenchmark`, `timeit`, `cProfile`) at L3+.

examples.text: A first script to summarise a small clinical trial table
A reusable function library for adverse-event coding lookups
A test suite catching a regression in a dose-conversion routine before production
Speeding up a slow PK/PD simulation by 50× through profiling and vectorisation
Reviewing and constraining LLM-generated analysis code for pharma compliance

competencies.name: Getting Started
descriptions: Recognise what code is and what an interpreter does; open a notebook and run an example.
Run and edit a short pharma script (e.g. summarise a CSV of adverse events) following a tutorial.
Set up a working analysis environment (Python or R, package manager, IDE) and produce a small reproducible script for a real pharma question.
— *(skill is fully covered by L3; further mastery shows up in other Programming competencies)*

competencies.name: Data and Variables
descriptions: Recognise basic data types (numbers, strings, booleans, dates) in pharma data.
Read a CSV/Excel/SAS file into Python or R and inspect types, missing values, and basic statistics.
Choose appropriate data structures (data frame, dict, list, factor) for a pharma analysis and avoid common type-coercion bugs (date parsing, factor encoding).
Design clean schemas for messy real-world pharma data and explain trade-offs (long vs. wide, factor vs. character, numeric precision).
Set conventions the team uses for types, encodings, and date/time handling across pharma projects.

competencies.name: Libraries
descriptions: Recognise that R/Python rely on packages and know a few core ones (`tidyverse`, `pandas`).
Install and load packages, follow examples from their docs to apply them to pharma data.
Choose appropriate libraries for a task (e.g. `survival` vs. `flexsurv`; `pandas` vs. `polars`) and combine them in an analysis.
Evaluate libraries by quality, license, maintenance, and validation status — relevant for pharma reproducibility and compliance.
Author or maintain an internal package, or contribute to a relevant open-source package used in pharma.

competencies.name: Functions
descriptions: Recognise function definitions and calls; explain inputs and outputs.
Write a small function (e.g. unit conversion for dosages) following an example.
Decompose a pharma analysis into well-named, testable functions with clear inputs and outputs.
Design APIs that survive change — sensible defaults, documented edge cases, careful handling of missing data.
Set the team's standards for function design and API style.

competencies.name: Loops and Branching
descriptions: Recognise `for`/`while` loops and `if`/`else` branches in pharma code.
Write loops and conditionals to iterate over a small list of records and apply rules.
Replace ad hoc loops with vectorised, mapped, or grouped operations where appropriate (`dplyr`, `purrr`, `pandas` `groupby`, `numpy`).
Choose the right control-flow shape for performance and clarity on real pharma data sizes; avoid common pitfalls (in-place mutation, off-by-one, hidden coercions).
— *(further mastery shows up in Code Optimization)*

competencies.name: Testing and Debugging
descriptions: Recognise an error traceback and read it to find the failing line.
Add `print` / `browser()` / a debugger and walk through a function on a small example.
Write unit tests (`pytest`, `testthat`) for pharma analysis code; reproduce a bug with a minimal example before fixing it.
Set up CI for an analysis package, including tests against representative pharma fixtures, and use coverage and property-based testing where it pays off.
Define the team's testing standards and validation expectations for code that touches regulated pharma data.

competencies.name: LLM Assisted Coding
descriptions: Recognise what an LLM coding assistant can and can't do, and the data-handling implications for pharma code.
Use an assistant to scaffold simple scripts and explain code; verify the output against documentation.
Use LLM assistants effectively for everyday pharma analysis work — generating code, refactoring, writing tests — while reading and validating every diff.
Constrain assistants for sensitive pharma contexts: ground them in real schemas, set up guardrails, audit and review generated code with a sceptical eye.
Define the team's policy and patterns for LLM-assisted coding in regulated pharma settings.

competencies.name: Code Optimization
descriptions: Recognise that some code is "slow" and that this can matter (cost, latency, deadlines).
Time a small piece of pharma code with `timeit` or `microbenchmark` and read the result.
Profile a real pharma analysis, identify the hot spot, and apply standard fixes (vectorisation, indexing, avoiding repeated I/O).
Re-architect a slow pharma pipeline (memory layout, parallelism, batching, columnar formats) for an order-of-magnitude speed-up while preserving correctness.
Set the team's performance standards and tooling for compute-heavy pharma workloads.

subareas.name: Workflow & Reproducibility
subareas.stack: Git, GitHub/GitLab; Quarto / R Markdown / Jupyter; `renv`, `uv`/`venv`, `conda`; Make / `targets` / Snakemake / Nextflow for pipelines; pre-commit hooks, code style (`ruff`, `lintr`, `styler`, `black`).

examples.text: A clinical analysis that runs end-to-end from raw inputs to a Quarto report with one command
A pull-request review that catches a silent data-filter change before it reaches a regulator
An internal style guide and pre-commit setup adopted across pharma teams
A `targets`/Nextflow pipeline that re-derives a regulatory submission deterministically months later

competencies.name: Documentation and Code Standards
descriptions: Recognise the difference between commented and uncommented code, and what a docstring is.
Add docstrings, README, and inline comments to a small pharma script, following examples.
Apply a style guide and lint/format tools across an analysis, and write documentation that lets a colleague reproduce the work.
Establish documentation patterns for a pharma project (analysis plan, data dictionary, decision log) and review others' work against them.
Define and own the team's coding and documentation standards.

competencies.name: Source Code (Version) Control Systems
descriptions: Recognise what Git is and read a commit history.
Clone, commit, push, and open a pull request on a small project, following a guide.
Use branches, pull requests, and code review fluently for everyday pharma analysis work; resolve typical merge conflicts.
Design a branching, review, and release strategy for a regulated pharma project (audit trail, signed commits, protected branches, traceable releases).
Set Git/CI conventions for the team or contribute to organisation-level standards.

competencies.name: Reproducible Analysis
descriptions: Recognise reasons that an analysis might not reproduce (random seed, hidden state, missing dependencies, non-deterministic inputs).
Run someone else's analysis from a clean checkout following the README, and report what's missing.
Build a literate, reproducible analysis (Quarto / R Markdown / Jupyter + locked environment) that another analyst can re-run from raw inputs.
Design a pipeline (`targets`, Snakemake, Nextflow, Make) that re-derives a regulatory or publication-grade output deterministically, with tests and provenance.
Define reproducibility standards for the team's regulated pharma work.

competencies.name: Collaboration
descriptions: Recognise the basic etiquette of shared codebases (don't commit to main, write a clear commit message).
Open a small pull request, respond to review comments, and merge once approved.
Review peers' pharma code with substantive, kind feedback; coordinate work across two or three contributors on the same analysis.
Lead a multi-person pharma analysis: scope, divide work, set up review and merge norms, unblock teammates.
Shape the collaboration culture across pharma analytics teams.

subareas.name: Critical Thinking
subareas.stack: general-purpose tooling — notebooks, dashboards, structured analysis-plan templates; bias and quality checklists.

examples.text: Spotting that an apparent treatment effect is driven by a coding change in the source EHR

tags.competency: Critical Thinking when working with data

examples.text: Recognising that a registry over-represents a particular site or population

tags.competency: Awareness of high level issues and challenges associated with data

examples.text: Writing a "pre-analysis questions" doc that surfaces likely biases before the analysis begins

tags.competency: Critical Thinking when working with data

competencies.name: Critical Thinking when working with data
descriptions: Recognise that data can be wrong, biased, or misleading even when it looks complete.
Apply a checklist to a pharma dataset: where did it come from, how was it collected, what's missing, what's been transformed.
Routinely interrogate a pharma dataset before analysis — origin, biases, exclusions, lineage — and document assumptions.
Recognise non-obvious data issues (informative missingness, regime change, coding drift, label leakage) and adjust analyses or design.
Define the team's habits and rituals for sceptical data work.

competencies.name: Awareness of high level issues and challenges associated with data
descriptions: Recognise common high-level pharma data challenges: missingness, fragmentation across sources, regulatory constraints, confounding.
Describe these challenges as they appear in a specific pharma dataset.
Anticipate these challenges in a new project and plan for them in the analysis design.
Map the data landscape for a pharma question across sources (clinical, real-world, genomic, regulatory) and reason about gaps.
Set strategy for how the org acquires, integrates, and reasons about pharma data over time.

subareas.name: Data Collection
subareas.stack: REDCap and similar EDC platforms; surveys; web/API ingestion (`httr2`, `requests`); registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, GBD, EMA); literature search tools.

examples.text: Designing a CRF that yields analysable data first time
Pulling structured trial outcomes from ClinicalTrials.gov by API
Building a search strategy across PubMed, Embase, and EU CTR for a meta-analysis

competencies.name: Data types
descriptions: Distinguish numeric, categorical, ordinal, date/time, and free-text data; recognise structured vs. unstructured.
Classify the variables in a pharma dataset and pick appropriate summaries.
Choose the right type and encoding for each variable in a new pharma dataset, including dates, units, and missingness conventions.
Design data type strategy for non-trivial pharma data (longitudinal, hierarchical, sparse, free text + codes).
Define standards for variable typing across the team's pharma datasets.

competencies.name: Data collection tools and methods
descriptions: Recognise the main pharma data collection methods: EDC, eCOA, surveys, APIs, registries, sensors.
Use one of these tools (e.g. REDCap or an HTTP API) to collect a small pharma dataset following an example.
Design and implement a data collection plan for a pharma study: instrument, fields, validation, exports.
Adapt collection to non-standard contexts (devices, multi-language eCOA, partner data, real-world streaming) and ensure quality at source.
Define the team's playbook for pharma data collection across study types.

competencies.name: Repositories and search methods
descriptions: Recognise the main pharma repositories (PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, EMA/FDA portals, EGA, dbGaP, GBD, real-world data vendors).
Run a basic search in one of them and download a structured result.
Build a reproducible, documented search strategy across multiple sources for a real pharma question.
Combine and deduplicate across repositories with awareness of bias and gaps; use programmatic APIs where it pays off.
Set the team's standards for systematic search and acquisition of pharma evidence.

subareas.name: Data Curation
subareas.stack: `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `pandas`, `polars`, `data.table`; controlled vocabularies (MedDRA, SNOMED CT, LOINC, ATC, RxNorm, ICD); validation tools (`pointblank`, `pandera`, `great_expectations`).

examples.text: Standardising adverse-event terms via MedDRA across studies
Reshaping a long-format lab dataset into per-patient summaries
Cleaning a pooled real-world dataset with ~30 source-specific quirks

competencies.name: Data standardization and transformation
descriptions: Recognise that the same concept can be encoded many ways across pharma sources (units, codes, formats).
Apply a mapping table or controlled vocabulary to a small dataset following an example.
Standardise a real pharma dataset using accepted vocabularies (MedDRA, ATC, LOINC, SNOMED) and document the mappings.
Design transformation strategies for messy multi-source pharma data with conflicting encodings and partial mappings.
Define the team's standardisation patterns and govern shared vocabularies and crosswalks.

competencies.name: Data conversion (between types)
descriptions: Recognise that converting between types (date, numeric, factor, character) can lose or distort information.
Convert types in a small dataset using `as.*` / `pd.to_*` functions, checking before and after.
Convert real pharma data between common shapes (long ↔ wide, JSON ↔ tabular, EAV ↔ wide) with explicit checks.
Handle non-trivial conversions (units, time zones, schema evolution) with auditable logic.
— *(further mastery covered by Standardization and by Integration in EMA)*

competencies.name: Data Cleaning
descriptions: Recognise common data quality issues — duplicates, impossible values, encoding errors, missing data patterns.
Apply standard cleaning steps to a small pharma dataset following a checklist.
Clean a real pharma dataset end-to-end with documented decisions, validations, and a record of what was changed and why.
Design cleaning logic for messy real-world or pooled pharma data, including informative missingness and regime change.
Set the team's standards and tooling for pharma data cleaning.

subareas.name: Data Organization
subareas.stack: relational databases (PostgreSQL, SQLite, DuckDB); columnar formats (Parquet, Arrow); CDISC SDTM/ADaM; metadata standards (Dublin Core, schema.org, CDISC Define-XML).

examples.text: Organising a study into clear "raw / intermediate / analysis" layers

tags.competency: Basic data organization methods and tools

examples.text: Designing a study-data SQL schema that survives protocol amendments
Authoring a Define-XML / data dictionary for a regulatory submission

tags.competency: Creation and use of meta data

competencies.name: Basic data organization methods and tools
descriptions: Recognise the difference between flat files, spreadsheets, and databases; know that "tidy data" is a thing.
Lay out a small pharma project's files and folders following a template.
Organise a pharma project into raw / intermediate / analysis layers with a clear file naming and folder convention.
Design data organisation for a multi-study, multi-team pharma programme.
Set the team's standards for project and data layout.

competencies.name: Database systems
descriptions: Recognise SQL, tables, joins, and indexes; explain why a database is sometimes better than CSV files.
Run basic SELECT/JOIN queries against a pharma data warehouse following examples.
Design and use a relational schema (or a DuckDB/SQLite store) for a real pharma project, with appropriate keys and indexes.
Tune queries on real pharma data; choose between relational, columnar, and document stores; reason about transactions and concurrency.
Define the team's data-platform patterns for pharma analytics.

competencies.name: Creation and use of meta data
descriptions: Recognise what metadata is — variable definitions, units, provenance, controlled vocabularies — and why pharma needs it.
Read and use a data dictionary or codebook for a pharma dataset.
Author a usable data dictionary for a real pharma dataset, including variable definitions, units, and provenance.
Apply CDISC Define-XML / SDTM/ADaM metadata for regulated submissions, or equivalent in another regime.
Define the team's metadata standards across studies.

subareas.name: Data Quality
subareas.stack: data validation frameworks (`pointblank`, `pandera`, `great_expectations`); checklists and quality dashboards; provenance tooling.

examples.text: A validation suite that fails the build when a study CSV ships a duplicate USUBJID
Rejecting a third-party real-world dataset whose source-coding drift can't be explained
A signed-off quality report for a regulatory submission

tags.competency: Evaluation of the quality of datasets

competencies.name: Data quality characteristics
descriptions: Recognise the standard quality dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness, provenance.
Describe these characteristics for a small pharma dataset.
Define quality criteria and acceptance thresholds for a real pharma dataset and check them.
Tailor quality definitions to the analytic purpose (a dataset can be "good enough" for one question and not another).
Set the team's data-quality framework and acceptance criteria.

competencies.name: Data Assessment
descriptions: Recognise basic data-profiling outputs (missingness, ranges, frequency tables).
Run a profiling tool on a pharma dataset and read the report.
Run a structured assessment of a real pharma dataset and report findings to stakeholders.
Design assessment that catches subtle issues — drift, leakage, informative missingness, source-coding change.
Set the team's standards and tooling for pharma data assessment.

competencies.name: Assessment of data sources(trustworthiness)
descriptions: Recognise that data sources differ in trustworthiness (e.g. peer-reviewed registry vs. scraped web data).
Describe a pharma data source's origin, governance, and known issues.
Assess a candidate pharma data source for fitness for a specific question — provenance, licence, coverage, biases.
Lead a vendor or partner data assessment for a regulated pharma context, including audits and contractual checks.
Define the team's vendor/source qualification framework.

competencies.name: Evaluation of the quality of datasets
descriptions: Recognise that "quality" is dataset-and-purpose specific.
Apply a quality scoring template to a small pharma dataset.
Produce a written quality evaluation of a pharma dataset for a specific analytic purpose.
Sign off (or reject) a dataset for regulated use with a defensible report; recommend remediation.
Set the team's evaluation standards and review process.

subareas.name: Data Security & Re-use
subareas.stack: access control (IAM, role-based access); secure storage (encrypted S3/Azure Blob); pseudonymisation/tokenisation; FAIR principles; DOI / data citation tooling; data-sharing platforms (Vivli, YODA, EGA, dbGaP, controlled-access registries).

examples.text: Pseudonymising a clinical dataset before sharing with an external statistician

tags.competency: Data classification, risk assessment, storage and backup

examples.text: Depositing trial data in Vivli with a DOI for downstream re-use

tags.competency: Methods and platforms for sharing data

examples.text: Setting an org-wide policy for trial-data sharing under EMA Policy 0070

competencies.name: Data classification, risk assessment, storage and backup
descriptions: Recognise data classification levels (public, internal, sensitive, regulated) and what each means for handling.
Apply the right storage and access controls to a small pharma dataset following policy.
Classify and protect a real pharma dataset: pseudonymisation, access control, encryption at rest, backups, retention.
Design risk-aware storage architectures for sensitive pharma data, with defensible audit trails.
Define the team's classification and security framework.

competencies.name: Data preservation and FAIR principles
descriptions: Recognise the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable).
Apply FAIR-aligned conventions (DOIs, persistent IDs, controlled vocabularies) to a small pharma dataset.
Make a real pharma dataset FAIR within its access constraints and deposit it in an appropriate repository.
Lead the FAIR-ification of a programme's data assets, including legacy datasets.
Define the team's FAIR-by-default standards and tooling.

competencies.name: Methods and platforms for sharing data
descriptions: Recognise the main pharma data-sharing platforms (Vivli, YODA, EGA, dbGaP, in-house) and their access models.
Submit or request a small dataset through one of these platforms, following the platform's guide.
Share or obtain a real pharma dataset through the right platform with appropriate consent, agreements, and controls.
Design sharing strategy for a study or programme balancing transparency, IP, consent, and regulation.
Set the team's sharing strategy and engage with platform/standards bodies.

competencies.name: Widely-accepted data citation methods
descriptions: Recognise data citation as a practice and recognise DOIs for datasets.
Cite a pharma dataset correctly in a report or paper following examples.
Mint and use DOIs / persistent identifiers for the team's pharma datasets and apply them in publications and submissions.
— *(further mastery is rare and folds into FAIR / Sharing competencies)*

subareas.name: Research Data Management
subareas.stack: Data Management Plan templates (DCC, NIH, Horizon Europe); CDISC where relevant; lab notebooks and ELN tooling.

examples.text: A study-level DMP that survives an EMA inspection
A repeatable DMP template adopted across the team

competencies.name: Data management plans
descriptions: Recognise what a Data Management Plan is and why funders and regulators require one.
Fill in a DMP template for a small pharma project from a worked example.
Author a complete, realistic DMP for a real pharma study and execute against it.
Author and maintain DMPs for regulated pharma studies through the full lifecycle, including amendments and audits.
Define the team's DMP templates, processes, and reviews.

subareas.name: Data Science Ethics
subareas.stack: organisational ethics codes; bias-detection tooling (`fairlearn`, `aequitas`); environmental footprint estimators (`codecarbon`); pharma-specific ethics guidance (CIOMS, Declaration of Helsinki).

examples.text: Catching that a model under-serves an under-represented patient subgroup

tags.competency: Bias in data science and algorithms

examples.text: Choosing between two analysis pipelines on energy/cost grounds at comparable accuracy

tags.competency: Environmental and social sustainability of data science practices

examples.text: Deciding not to ship a feature because of a foreseeable downstream harm

tags.competency: Ethical dilemmas in pharmaceutical data science

competencies.name: Concepts in data science ethics
descriptions: Recognise the core concepts: consent, privacy, fairness, accountability, transparency, dual use.
Describe these concepts as they apply to a specific pharma project.
Apply ethics frameworks routinely in pharma project decisions and document the reasoning.
Recognise non-obvious ethical issues (proxy variables, group privacy, deployment harms) and act on them.
Lead the team's ethics practice and contribute to organisation- or industry-level standards.

competencies.name: Bias in data science and algorithms
descriptions: Recognise sources of bias: sampling, measurement, label, deployment, historical.
Apply a bias checklist to a pharma dataset or model output.
Quantify and report subgroup performance and bias for a real pharma model, and act on the results.
Diagnose and mitigate bias in non-trivial pharma settings (intersectional subgroups, label noise, deployment shift).
Set the team's standards for bias measurement and mitigation in pharma analytics.

competencies.name: Environmental and social sustainability of data science practices
descriptions: Recognise that compute, storage, and modelling choices have environmental and social costs.
Estimate the energy or compute cost of a pharma analysis using simple tooling.
Choose between approaches partly on sustainability grounds in pharma projects (right-sized models, efficient pipelines, regional compute).
Lead sustainability-aware design for compute-heavy pharma workloads.
Set the team's sustainability practices.

competencies.name: Ethical dilemmas in pharmaceutical data science
descriptions: Recognise common pharma-specific dilemmas (off-label inference, drug repurposing risks, consent for secondary use, dual-use research).
Describe a pharma dilemma and the relevant stakeholders.
Reason through a real pharma dilemma using an ethics framework, document the decision, and consult appropriately.
Lead the resolution of complex pharma ethics dilemmas with cross-functional input (clinical, legal, patient advocacy).
Help shape organisational or industry positions on pharma data ethics.

subareas.name: Legislation
subareas.stack: GDPR, HIPAA, GxP, EMA/FDA guidance, ICH E6/E9, EU AI Act; country-specific health-data laws; copyright and licensing frameworks.

examples.text: Choosing a lawful basis under GDPR for a real-world data study
Negotiating data licences for a multi-source meta-analysis
Preparing for an EMA inspection of an analysis pipeline

competencies.name: Central legal and regulatory frameworks
descriptions: Recognise the main frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, GxP, ICH, EMA/FDA guidance, EU AI Act) and what they govern.
Identify which frameworks apply to a given pharma project at a high level.
Apply the relevant frameworks routinely in a pharma analytics project — design choices, documentation, controls.
Lead compliance for a complex pharma project involving multiple jurisdictions or evolving regulation (e.g. EU AI Act applied to a clinical model).
Engage with regulators and shape the team's compliance posture.

competencies.name: Copyright and intellectual property concerns
descriptions: Recognise that data, code, and models can be subject to copyright, licensing, patents, and trade secrets.
Read a dataset or library licence and explain what it permits.
Apply correct licensing and IP handling to a real pharma project (data, code, model artefacts).
Negotiate or design IP arrangements for collaborative pharma work and unusual data uses.
Define the team's IP and licensing strategy.

subareas.name: Privacy
subareas.stack: pseudonymisation/de-identification tools; access control and audit; informed-consent platforms; differential privacy and synthetic data tooling at higher levels; AI transparency documentation (model cards, datasheets, EU AI Act records).

examples.text: Proper de-identification of a registry dataset before secondary analysis

tags.competency: Knowledge and compliance with privacy and data security regulations

tags.competency: Ensure that AI systems used are transparent and aligned with legal and ethical norms

competencies.name: Knowledge and compliance with privacy and data security regulations
descriptions: Recognise the main privacy regulations relevant to pharma (GDPR, HIPAA, country-specific health-data laws) at a high level.
Apply standard privacy controls (access, encryption, pseudonymisation) to a small dataset following policy.
Run a real pharma project under the relevant privacy regulations end-to-end, with documented controls.
Design privacy strategy for a complex pharma project (multi-jurisdiction, real-world data, partner sharing).
Set the team's privacy practices and engage with DPOs and regulators.

competencies.name: Design and implementation of respectful and legal informed consent processes
descriptions: Recognise the elements of valid informed consent for pharma research.
Read an existing consent form / process and identify its main elements.
Implement a consent process for a pharma study that meets legal and ethical requirements and is genuinely respectful.
Design consent for novel pharma contexts (digital biomarkers, secondary use, dynamic consent, vulnerable populations).
Define the team's consent standards and contribute to organisational practice.

competencies.name: Act with integrity when handling sensitive data
descriptions: Recognise that sensitive pharma data (patient identifiers, genomics, mental health) requires elevated care.
Follow the team's handling rules for sensitive data in a small project.
Routinely apply sensitivity-appropriate handling — minimisation, segregation, access logs, secure transfer — across pharma work.
Lead the integrity practice on a sensitive pharma programme, including audits and incident response.
Set the team's integrity expectations and culture.

competencies.name: Application of legal and ethical standards to ensure responsible and competent data handling
descriptions: Recognise that legal and ethical standards translate into concrete handling requirements.
Apply the team's standard checklist to a small pharma dataset.
Operate consistently within applicable legal and ethical standards on a real pharma project, with traceable decisions.
Resolve novel cases where standards are silent or in tension, with appropriate consultation.
Define and maintain the team's combined legal-and-ethical handling framework.

competencies.name: Ensure that AI systems used are transparent and aligned with legal and ethical norms
descriptions: Recognise the AI-specific transparency expectations (intended use, limitations, risk class under EU AI Act, model cards).
Read or fill out a model card for an existing AI tool.
Document an AI system used in a pharma context: purpose, data, evaluation, limitations, risks, monitoring.
Design and govern AI deployment in pharma to meet evolving regulation (EU AI Act, FDA guidance) and internal ethics review.
Set the team's AI governance standards and engage externally.

competencies.name: Continuously update knowledge of ethical, legal, and technological developments in PDS
descriptions: Recognise that ethics, law, and tech are moving fast in PDS and that yesterday's answer may not still hold.
Follow at least one credible source (newsletter, regulator update, professional body) regularly.
Maintain working knowledge across ethics, law, and tech and bring relevant updates into the team's practice.
Lead horizon-scanning for the team and translate developments into concrete changes.
Help shape the field externally — talks, working groups, publications.

subareas.name: (Critical) Evaluation
subareas.stack: statistical and ML evaluation tooling (`tidymodels`, `scikit-learn` metrics, `dowhy`, `causalml`); reproducibility tools; bias and robustness checklists; sensitivity analysis frameworks.

examples.text: Stating, before unblinding, the assumptions a trial analysis depends on
Distinguishing association from causation in a real-world effectiveness analysis
Showing that a predictive model degrades on a held-out hospital and choosing not to deploy

competencies.name: Study design & assumptions
descriptions: Recognise that every analysis rests on assumptions about design and data.
Read a study protocol or analysis plan and list its main assumptions.
State and check the assumptions of a real pharma analysis explicitly.
Adapt designs and assumption-checking when reality differs from the protocol (missing strata, protocol deviations, regime change).
Set the team's standards for documenting and challenging assumptions.

competencies.name: Association & inference
descriptions: Recognise the difference between association and causation; recognise statistical inference as a distinct activity.
Run a basic association test on a pharma dataset following an example.
Choose appropriate inferential methods for a real pharma question and interpret them honestly.
Handle non-trivial inference (clustering, multiple comparisons, time-varying confounders) competently.
Set the team's inference standards.

competencies.name: Causal inference & sensitivity
descriptions: Recognise that observational pharma data alone usually doesn't give causal answers; recognise core ideas (confounding, counterfactuals, DAGs).
Read a DAG and a propensity-score analysis and explain its logic.
Apply standard causal inference methods (matching, IPTW, instrumental variables, target trial emulation) to a real pharma question.
Run defensible sensitivity analyses (E-values, tipping-point, negative controls) and act on them.
Lead causal-methods practice in the team or contribute to the field.

competencies.name: Model evaluation & robustness
descriptions: Recognise basic evaluation metrics (accuracy, AUC, calibration, RMSE) and what they do and don't tell you.
Compute standard metrics on a small pharma model following an example.
Evaluate a real pharma model with appropriate metrics, calibration, and held-out data; report transparently.
Stress-test a pharma model — subgroup performance, distribution shift, adversarial inputs — and decide whether it should ship.
Set the team's model-evaluation standards for pharma.

competencies.name: Reproducibility
descriptions: Recognise that an analysis must be reproducible to be trustworthy.
Re-run a peer's pharma analysis from a clean checkout.
Make a real pharma analysis reproducible end-to-end (env, seeds, pipeline, data lineage).
Achieve reproducibility under hard constraints (controlled-access data, regulated environments, multi-team handoffs).
Set the team's reproducibility expectations and tooling.

competencies.name: Limitations & Uncertainty
descriptions: Recognise that every pharma analysis has limitations and that point estimates without uncertainty are usually misleading.
Add confidence intervals or prediction intervals to a small pharma analysis.
Communicate limitations and uncertainty honestly in real pharma analyses to mixed audiences.
Quantify and propagate uncertainty in non-trivial pharma settings (Bayesian, bootstrap, simulation, decision analysis).
Set the team's standards for communicating limitations and uncertainty.

competencies.name: Transportability & fairness
descriptions: Recognise that a model fit on one pharma population may not work on another, and that this matters for fairness.
Compare a pharma model's performance across two subgroups or sites following an example.
Routinely evaluate transportability and subgroup fairness for real pharma models, and act on findings.
Diagnose and address transportability and fairness problems in deployment (recalibration, domain adaptation, refusal-to-deploy).
Set the team's transportability and fairness standards.

subareas.name: Analysis
subareas.stack: R (`tidyverse`, `survival`, `tidymodels`, `flexsurv`, `nlmixr`/`mrgsolve`), Python (`pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `lifelines`, `statsmodels`); domain-specific PK/PD tools (NONMEM, Monolix where applicable).

examples.text: A pre-specified hypothesis test for a primary trial endpoint
A population PK/PD model fit to a phase-2 study
A survival analysis of time-to-progression with competing risks
Feature selection for a high-dimensional biomarker model with proper resampling

competencies.name: Qualitative and quantitative analysis
descriptions: Recognise the difference between qualitative and quantitative methods and when each is appropriate.
Run basic descriptive analyses on a small pharma dataset following an example.
Choose and apply qualitative or quantitative methods appropriately to a real pharma question.
Combine qualitative and quantitative evidence (e.g. clinician interviews + outcomes data) into a coherent pharma analysis.
Set the team's standards for mixed-methods pharma analysis.

competencies.name: Hypothesis testing
descriptions: Recognise null/alternative hypotheses, type I/II error, p-values, and confidence intervals.
Run a t-test, χ², or simple regression test on a pharma sample following an example.
Choose and run an appropriate test for a real pharma question and interpret it honestly (effect size, CIs, multiplicity).
Handle non-trivial testing (group sequential, multiple endpoints, non-inferiority, Bayesian alternatives) competently.
Set the team's standards for hypothesis testing in pharma.

competencies.name: PK/PD & exposure-response
descriptions: Recognise the basic concepts: absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination, exposure–response.
Read and interpret a basic PK/PD plot or model output.
Fit standard PK/PD models with appropriate tooling on a real pharma dataset and interpret the results.
Build population PK/PD or exposure–response models that inform real dosing decisions; handle data quirks and covariates.
Lead PK/PD modelling practice in the team or contribute to methods development.

competencies.name: Modelling
descriptions: Recognise statistical modelling as a distinct activity from raw analysis or ML.
Fit a linear or logistic model to a small pharma dataset following an example.
Choose and fit appropriate models (mixed-effects, GLM, GAM, survival) for real pharma questions and validate them.
Handle non-trivial modelling (hierarchical, longitudinal, joint models, missing-data methods) on real pharma data.
Set the team's modelling standards or contribute to methods.

competencies.name: Survival analysis
descriptions: Recognise survival data, censoring, hazard, and Kaplan–Meier curves.
Fit a Kaplan–Meier curve and a Cox model on a pharma sample following an example.
Choose and apply standard survival methods to real pharma data (Cox, parametric, stratified) and check assumptions.
Handle non-trivial survival analyses (competing risks, time-varying covariates, joint longitudinal–survival, frailty) on real pharma data.
Set the team's standards for time-to-event analysis.

competencies.name: Feature selection & dimensionality reduction
descriptions: Recognise why high-dimensional pharma data needs reduction (multicollinearity, overfitting, interpretability).
Run PCA or basic regularisation on a pharma sample following an example.
Choose appropriate selection / reduction methods for a real pharma model and interpret them.
Apply principled selection (stability, nested CV, domain-informed) to high-dimensional pharma data without leaking information.
Set the team's standards for feature engineering and reduction in pharma ML.

competencies.name: Resampling design & class imbalance
descriptions: Recognise cross-validation, bootstrap, and class imbalance as concepts.
Run k-fold CV and a simple class-rebalancing step on a pharma model following an example.
Design appropriate resampling for a real pharma problem (grouped CV, stratified, time-aware) and address imbalance honestly.
Handle non-trivial resampling pitfalls — leakage, dependent samples, rare events — and choose calibration strategies.
Set the team's resampling and validation standards.

subareas.name: Exploration
subareas.stack: EDA tooling — `tidyverse`/`pandas`/`polars`, `ggplot2`/`plotly`, `skimr`/`pandas-profiling`/`ydata-profiling`; clustering and dimensionality reduction libraries (`uwot`, `umap-learn`, `scikit-learn`, `dbscan`); time-series tooling.

examples.text: A first-pass profiling report on a new real-world dataset that surfaces three blocking issues
Reframing a stalled "predict adherence" project as a cohort-definition problem
UMAP + clustering on a multi-omics cohort that suggests a novel sub-phenotype

competencies.name: Profiling & quality
descriptions: Recognise that EDA / profiling comes before modelling.
Generate a profiling report on a pharma dataset and read it.
Run a thorough profiling pass on a real pharma dataset and turn findings into analysis decisions.
Design profiling that catches subtle problems (drift, informative missingness, source-coding change).
Set the team's EDA standards and tooling.

competencies.name: Problem framing
descriptions: Recognise that the framing of a question shapes the answer and the data needed.
Restate a pharma question in analytic terms (target, population, time horizon, outcome) following examples.
Frame a real pharma question into a tractable analysis with clear scope, exclusions, and metrics.
Reframe stuck or ill-posed pharma questions into ones that can be answered with the available evidence.
Coach the team on framing and shape how problems enter the pipeline.

competencies.name: Clustering & proximity analyses
descriptions: Recognise clustering as a way to find structure in unlabelled pharma data.
Run k-means or hierarchical clustering on a pharma sample following an example.
Choose and apply appropriate clustering methods for real pharma data and validate the results.
Handle hard cases — high-dimensional, mixed-type, large-scale — with stable, interpretable clusters.
Lead clustering practice in the team or contribute methods.

competencies.name: Distributional statistical data analysis (EDA)
descriptions: Recognise distributions, summary statistics, and the value of looking before testing.
Plot distributions and compute summaries on a pharma sample following an example.
Run distributional EDA on real pharma data and let it inform method choice.
Detect non-trivial distributional issues (mixture, heavy tails, regime change, censoring) and adapt analysis.
Set EDA standards in the team.

competencies.name: High-dimensional screening
descriptions: Recognise the multiple-comparisons and dimensionality challenges in pharma omics and similar data.
Run a basic screen with multiple-comparison correction following an example.
Run a defensible high-dimensional screen on real pharma data with appropriate controls.
Apply principled high-dimensional methods (sparsity, knockoffs, FDR, stability selection) to pharma data.
Lead high-dimensional analytics practice or contribute methods.

competencies.name: Time-aware EDA
descriptions: Recognise that time-indexed pharma data (vitals, claims, dosing, adverse events) needs time-aware EDA.
Plot time-series and rolling summaries for a small pharma sample.
Run time-aware EDA on real pharma data — seasonality, drift, gaps, censoring — and act on it.
Handle complex temporal pharma data (irregular sampling, multiple time scales, survival/longitudinal mixes).
Set the team's standards for temporal EDA.

competencies.name: Cohort & episode definition
descriptions: Recognise that cohorts and episodes have to be explicitly defined; small definition changes can move results.
Apply an existing cohort/episode definition to a pharma dataset following an example.
Define a real pharma cohort or episode (inclusion/exclusion, index date, look-back, follow-up) and document trade-offs.
Handle non-trivial definitions (target trial emulation, competing exposures, multi-source consistency).
Set the team's cohort/episode standards and review process.

subareas.name: Integration
subareas.stack: ETL tooling (`dplyr`, `pandas`, `polars`, `dbt`); record linkage (`reclin2`, `recordlinkage`); ontology mapping (OHDSI / OMOP CDM, FHIR); provenance and lineage tooling.

examples.text: Linking a clinical trial dataset with insurance claims for follow-up outcomes
Mapping a study dataset to OMOP for cross-org analytics
Engineering pharma-specific features (washout windows, dose intensity, switching) for a model

competencies.name: Data integration & harmonisation
descriptions: Recognise that real pharma analyses usually combine sources that don't agree on definitions.
Join two small pharma datasets on a known key, checking row counts and unmatched records.
Integrate real pharma sources end-to-end with documented harmonisation choices and quality checks.
Lead harmonisation across messy multi-source pharma data with conflicting encodings, partial overlap, and quality issues.
Set the team's integration patterns.

competencies.name: Standards & interoperability
descriptions: Recognise the main pharma standards (CDISC SDTM/ADaM, OMOP, FHIR, HL7, MedDRA) and what they cover.
Map a small pharma dataset to one standard following an example.
Apply standards correctly in a real pharma project (submission, common data model, partner exchange).
Lead a standards adoption or migration (e.g. a real OMOP migration of legacy studies) and engage with standards bodies.
Define the team's standards strategy.

competencies.name: Feature engineering (domain specific)
descriptions: Recognise that pharma features (washout, dose intensity, treatment switching, time on therapy) need domain-aware construction.
Implement a small pharma feature following a worked example.
Engineer pharma-specific features for a real model with clear definitions, time-respect, and unit tests.
Design feature sets that survive deployment shifts and respect causal structure (no leakage, no future information).
Set the team's feature-engineering patterns and shared feature stores.

competencies.name: Provenance, lineage, & linkage
descriptions: Recognise provenance and lineage as separate concerns from analysis logic.
Read a lineage diagram for an existing pharma pipeline.
Maintain provenance and lineage for a real pharma analysis end-to-end (raw → derived → results) and link records across sources.
Design lineage and linkage that meets regulatory expectations and survives data refreshes and retroactive corrections.
Set the team's lineage and linkage architecture.

subareas.name: Mining
subareas.stack: classic mining (`arules`, `mlxtend`); NLP (`spaCy`, `udpipe`, `tidytext`, transformers); graph analytics (`igraph`, `networkx`, `tidygraph`); time-series and process mining (`prophet`, `tsfeatures`, `pm4py`).

examples.text: Mining adverse-event term co-occurrence in spontaneous reports
Information extraction from oncology pathology reports
Treatment-pathway analysis from claims using process mining

competencies.name: Sources identification
descriptions: Recognise the main mineable pharma sources (EHR, claims, registries, literature, social media, sensor streams).
Describe a single pharma source: structure, biases, access route.
Identify and qualify the right mining sources for a real pharma question.
Combine multiple sources into a defensible mining design with awareness of biases and gaps.
Set the team's source-identification practice.

competencies.name: Pattern/association rule mining
descriptions: Recognise association rules and itemset / co-occurrence mining.
Run a small `arules`/`mlxtend` analysis on a pharma sample following an example.
Apply association mining to a real pharma question (co-prescribing, AE co-occurrence) with appropriate filters and interpretation.
Handle non-trivial mining (rare events, hierarchical items, statistical correction) on real pharma data.
— *(further mastery folds into broader Mining or Modelling competencies)*

competencies.name: Text mining (NLP) & information extraction
descriptions: Recognise NLP tasks relevant to pharma: classification, NER, normalisation to ontologies.
Run a basic NLP pipeline (tokenisation, NER) on pharma text following an example.
Apply NLP to a real pharma question (extracting outcomes, adverse events, eligibility from clinical text) with evaluation.
Handle hard pharma NLP — domain adaptation, noisy text, multilingual data, weak supervision, LLM-assisted extraction with validation.
Lead pharma NLP practice or contribute methods.

competencies.name: Graph/network-based mining
descriptions: Recognise graphs / networks (drug–target, co-prescription, citation) as a mining substrate.
Build and visualise a small pharma graph following an example.
Run graph algorithms (centrality, community detection) on real pharma networks and interpret results.
Apply advanced graph methods (graph ML, link prediction) to real pharma problems with careful evaluation.
Lead graph-analytics practice in the team.

competencies.name: Time-series & process mining
descriptions: Recognise time-series forecasting and process mining as distinct disciplines.
Fit a basic time-series model or run a simple process-mining tool on pharma data following an example.
Apply time-series or process mining to a real pharma question (treatment pathways, adverse-event trends, sensor signals).
Handle hard cases — irregular sampling, regime change, multiple time scales, complex pathways — defensibly.
Set the team's standards for temporal and process analytics.

subareas.name: ML & AI Foundations
subareas.stack: `scikit-learn`, `tidymodels`, `xgboost`/`lightgbm`/`catboost`, PyTorch / Keras / `torch` for R; `mlflow` / `wandb` for tracking; standard reinforcement-learning toolkits where relevant.

examples.text: A supervised model predicting 30-day readmission, with proper evaluation
Discovering subtypes in a pooled biomarker dataset
A deep model for medical image segmentation in pathology

competencies.name: ML algorithms
descriptions: Recognise the major algorithm families: linear/logistic, tree-based, kernel methods, neural nets, clustering.
Train a default `scikit-learn` / `tidymodels` model on a pharma sample following an example.
Choose and tune an appropriate algorithm for a real pharma problem with honest evaluation.
Choose between algorithms on real pharma data based on data shape, interpretability, regulation, and deployment constraints.
Set the team's algorithm patterns and contribute to methods.

competencies.name: AI versus ML
descriptions: Distinguish AI, ML, statistics, and rule-based systems at a high level.
Place a given pharma tool in the right bucket and explain why.
Communicate the distinction clearly to non-technical pharma stakeholders and use it to set realistic expectations.
— *(skill is conceptual; further mastery shows up in other ML/AI competencies)*

competencies.name: Supervised learning
descriptions: Recognise classification and regression as supervised tasks; recognise train/validation/test splits.
Train and evaluate a basic classifier or regressor on a pharma sample following an example.
Build a real supervised pharma model end-to-end with appropriate evaluation, calibration, and reporting.
Handle hard supervised cases (rare outcomes, censoring, label noise, distribution shift) on real pharma data.
Set the team's standards for supervised pharma modelling.

competencies.name: Unsupervised learning
descriptions: Recognise unsupervised tasks (clustering, density estimation, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction).
Run a basic unsupervised method on a pharma sample following an example.
Apply unsupervised methods to a real pharma question and validate the results sensibly.
Handle complex unsupervised problems on real pharma data (mixed types, high dimensions, weak labels).
Lead unsupervised-methods practice in the team.

competencies.name: Deep Learning
descriptions: Recognise deep learning and the main architectures (CNNs, transformers, RNNs).
Train a small model in PyTorch / Keras on a pharma sample following an example.
Build a real deep model for a pharma task (imaging, sequence, signal) with appropriate evaluation.
Handle hard deep-learning cases on pharma data — domain shift, limited labels, regulation, validation — credibly.
Lead deep-learning practice in the team or contribute methods.

competencies.name: Reinforcement learning
descriptions: Recognise RL and where it might apply in pharma (adaptive trials, dynamic treatment regimes, dosing).
Read a published pharma RL example and explain its setup.
Apply RL to a tractable pharma simulation problem (e.g. dosing optimisation in silico) with honest evaluation.
Lead an RL pharma application with proper safety, evaluation, and translational thinking.
— *(rare; folds into research / methods leadership)*

subareas.name: Model Building & Assessment
subareas.stack: explainability and interpretation tooling (`shap`, `lime`, `iml`, `tidymodels` parsnip + workflows); robust evaluation harnesses; uncertainty quantification (`conformalInference`, Bayesian tooling); optimisation theory awareness.

examples.text: A SHAP analysis that reveals a model relying on a leaky proxy variable
A sensitivity analysis varying preprocessing choices to test robustness
A held-out external-site evaluation that decides whether to deploy

competencies.name: Model interpretation
descriptions: Recognise that model behaviour can and should be inspected, not taken on trust.
Run a SHAP/LIME / variable-importance analysis on a small pharma model following an example.
Interpret a real pharma model with appropriate methods and explain it to stakeholders honestly.
Use interpretation to spot real problems (leakage, spurious features, subgroup failure) and act on them.
Set the team's interpretation practice for pharma ML.

competencies.name: Model assessment and sensitivity analysis
descriptions: Recognise that single point-estimates of performance hide a lot.
Run a basic sensitivity check (e.g. swap a hyperparameter) on a pharma model following an example.
Build assessment and sensitivity analysis into real pharma modelling: bootstrap, subgroup, design choices.
Stress-test pharma models systematically (data quirks, design choices, distribution shift) and report defensibly.
Set the team's assessment and sensitivity standards.

competencies.name: Importance of robust evaluation
descriptions: Recognise that evaluation choices can swing conclusions and that robust evaluation is non-negotiable in pharma.
Apply a robust evaluation template (held-out, CV, calibration, subgroup) to a small pharma model.
Design robust evaluation for a real pharma model and report it transparently.
Handle non-trivial evaluation contexts (external sites, prospective use, regulatory expectations) credibly.
Set the team's evaluation standards.

competencies.name: Challenges for machine learning
descriptions: Recognise common ML failure modes — overfitting, leakage, distribution shift, label noise, bias.
Spot one of these failure modes in a pharma example following a checklist.
Diagnose and mitigate these failure modes in real pharma models.
Anticipate failure modes from project design and instrument for them ahead of time.
Set the team's defensive ML practices for pharma.

competencies.name: Learning algorithms as principled optimization approaches
descriptions: Recognise that ML algorithms are usually solving an optimisation problem with assumptions and trade-offs.
Read a loss function and explain what it is optimising on a pharma example.
Choose and modify loss functions / regularisers appropriately for a real pharma problem.
Reason about optimisation behaviour in pharma ML (convergence, identifiability, conditioning) and act on it.
Contribute methods or set the team's principled-optimisation practice.

subareas.name: Use of AI in Education & Research
subareas.stack: general-purpose LLMs (Claude, GPT-class) and coding assistants; retrieval-augmented setups for pharma corpora; evaluation tooling for AI outputs; internal usage policies.

examples.text: Drafting an analysis plan with an LLM and editing it with a sceptical reviewer's eye

tags.competency: What can AI be used for? What can it not be used for?

examples.text: Recognising and correcting LLM hallucinations in a literature summary
An internal policy that distinguishes safe and unsafe LLM use cases for pharma work

tags.competency: What can AI be used for? What can it not be used for?

competencies.name: What can AI be used for? What can it not be used for?
descriptions: Recognise the general capabilities and limits of current AI (LLMs and others) at a high level.
Place a candidate pharma use case on a "good fit / poor fit / unsafe" map following examples.
Decide AI use case-by-case in real pharma work, with clear rationale and guardrails.
Lead AI strategy for a pharma team, balancing value, safety, and regulation.
Define organisational policy and engage externally on responsible AI use in pharma.

competencies.name: Efficient prompting
descriptions: Recognise that prompting affects output quality.
Use a simple prompting template (role, task, constraints, examples) on a pharma task following an example.
Routinely produce useful pharma outputs with LLMs through structured prompting, retrieval, and verification.
Engineer prompts and small workflows that survive deployment in pharma settings (evaluation, guardrails, retrieval grounding).
Set the team's prompting and AI-workflow patterns.

competencies.name: Common misconceptions about generative AI
descriptions: Recognise common misconceptions: that LLMs "know" things, that fluent text means correct text, that bigger model means safer model.
Spot a misconception in a pharma example following a checklist.
Routinely correct misconceptions in pharma colleagues' use of generative AI.
Help non-technical pharma audiences calibrate their trust in generative AI in their actual workflows.
Lead the team's communication and education on generative-AI realities.

subareas.name: Mathematics
subareas.stack: pen-and-paper / whiteboard; `numpy`/`scipy.linalg`, `sympy`, R `Matrix`; optimisation libraries (`optim`, `scipy.optimize`, `cvxpy`).

examples.text: Reasoning about why a gradient-based optimiser fails to converge on a particular PK model
Hand-deriving the linear-algebra structure behind a PCA on omics data
Setting up a constrained optimisation for a dosing-decision problem

competencies.name: Set theory and basic logic
descriptions: Recognise basic set operations and Boolean logic.
Apply them to filter / combine pharma datasets following examples.
Reason fluently about sets, logic, and conditions when defining cohorts, exclusions, and rules.
— *(further mastery shows up in cohort definition and data-engineering competencies)*

competencies.name: Quantitative reasoning
descriptions: Recognise basic quantitative concepts (rates, proportions, percentages, units, magnitudes).
Compute and sense-check basic quantities for a pharma dataset.
Reason quantitatively about real pharma data — sanity-check numbers, spot magnitude errors, communicate clearly.
Build quantitative intuition for non-trivial pharma problems (rates, exposures, hazards, costs).
Coach the team on quantitative thinking.

competencies.name: Basic calculus and linear algebra plus matrices
descriptions: Recognise vectors, matrices, derivatives, and integrals as objects.
Compute basic operations (matrix multiply, derivative of a polynomial) following examples.
Apply basic linear algebra and calculus comfortably to pharma analytics (regression, transformations, gradients).
— *(progresses into Multivariate calculus, Advanced linear algebra)*

competencies.name: Basic differentiation and integration
descriptions: Recognise differentiation and integration as concepts.
Compute simple derivatives and integrals following examples.
Apply basic differentiation and integration where they show up in pharma analyses (rate calculations, AUC).
— *(progresses into Multivariate calculus)*

competencies.name: Partial derivatives
descriptions: Recognise partial derivatives and gradients.
Compute partial derivatives of small functions following examples.
Use partial derivatives in pharma analyses — gradient-based fitting, sensitivity, marginal effects.
Reason about gradient behaviour in non-trivial pharma models (identifiability, conditioning).
— *(rare; subsumed by Optimization / Multivariate calculus mastery)*

competencies.name: Multivariate calculus
descriptions: Recognise multivariate calculus concepts (Jacobians, Hessians, chain rule).
Apply them to small problems following examples.
Use multivariate calculus where pharma modelling needs it (gradient methods, delta method, sensitivity).
Diagnose and fix optimisation/inference issues in pharma models that come from calculus structure.
Contribute methods or coach the team on multivariate methods.

competencies.name: Advanced linear algebra
descriptions: Recognise advanced concepts (eigendecomposition, SVD, projections, pseudo-inverses).
Apply them in small pharma problems following examples.
Use them confidently in pharma analyses (PCA, latent models, regularisation).
Reason about numerical conditioning and stability for real pharma matrices (ill-conditioned designs, sparse covariates).
Contribute methods or coach the team.

competencies.name: Optimization
descriptions: Recognise optimisation problems (objective, constraints, variables) and standard solvers.
Solve a small constrained / unconstrained problem with `scipy.optimize` or R `optim` following examples.
Formulate and solve real pharma optimisation problems (dose finding, design optimisation, model fitting).
Choose between solvers and formulations for hard pharma optimisation; diagnose convergence issues; handle non-convexity.
Contribute methods or coach the team on pharma optimisation.

subareas.name: Statistical thinking
subareas.stack: the same R/Python statistical stack as Statistics; the differentiator is mindset and habits (study design, uncertainty, falsifiability).

examples.text: Reframing a "how big is X?" pharma question into a falsifiable, prespecified analysis
Coaching a junior on the difference between "the data says" and "the model says"

competencies.name: Statistical thinking
descriptions: Recognise statistical thinking as a habit (think about variability, design, and uncertainty before computing).
Apply a basic checklist (population, sample, design, uncertainty) to a pharma question.
Routinely think statistically about real pharma problems — what could vary, what's prespecified, what's exploratory.
